title: Anirudh Goyal (@anirudhg9119)
summary:
Where do learning signals come from when there's no ground truth ?
Compute as Teacher: Convert the model's exploration at inference time into reference free supervision.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G1xNX9iW4AAn3uk.jpg
Quoting @DulhanJay
🚨New Meta Superintelligence Labs Paper🚨
What do we do when we don’t have reference answers for RL? What if annotations are too expensive or unknown? Compute as Teacher (CaT🐈) turns inference compute into a post-training supervision signal. CaT improves up to 30% even on non-verifiable domains (HealthBench) across 3 model families.
In CaT, the model self-synthesises existing GRPO rollouts into a high quality answer, reconciling disagreements, partial solutions, and facts. We use this estimated reference to reward each individual rollout, converting more inference compute into supervision for RL!
As training progresses, the quality of rollouts, and the estimate reference, keep on increasing, with the model learning from experience 🔄
Without any thinking tokens, across Llama, Gemma, Qwen we find large improvements on both MATH and HealthBench!
How does CaT work for non-verifiable domains? A frozen copy of the model generates a rubric from the estimated reference, allowing automated rewards with an LLM that checks each criterion. We show this outperforms both SFT and direct LLM judgements.
As an inference-time technique, the synthesis in CaT outperforms majority voting and self-selected best-of-N. This is because CaT doesn't just select, it reconciles. It can even disagree with answers of individual rollouts, combining them to produce a better one!
Beyond synthesis, generating supervision opens the door to learning from any inference-time methods we develop in the future! It's bitter-lesson friendly 📈
Paper, and thread below 👇
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G1Iwo67XkAA7bCB.jpg

The thing that is exciting *to me* about @AnthropicAI's "agent skills" announcement is that it provides a step toward continual learning.
- Rather than continuously updating model weights, agents interacting with the world can continuously add new skills.
- Compute spent on reasoning can serve a dual purpose of generating new skills (right now the work that goes into reasoning is largely discarded after a task is performed).
I imagine vast amounts of knowledge and skills will be stored outside of a model's weights. It seems natural to distill some of that knowledge into model weights over time, but that part seems less fundamental to me.
There are many nice things about storing knowledge outside of the model
- It's interpretable (just read through the skills)
- You can correct mistakes (the skills / knowledge are in plaintext, so are easy to update)
- Should be highly data efficient (in the same way that in-context learning is data efficient)

title: Anirudh Goyal (@anirudhg9119)
summary:
Best possible task accuracy after fixing constraints on inference process? Tokens across all generations, depth of generation chain (“latency”), total context length and compute.
PDR achieves pareto frontier: "draft in parallel → distill to a compact workspace → refine".
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G8OpdRgWoAYclti.jpg
Quoting @dair_ai
NEW Research from Meta Superintelligence Labs and collaborators.
The default approach to improving LLM reasoning today remains extending chain-of-thought sequences.
Longer reasoning traces aren't always better. Longer traces conflate reasoning depth with sequence length and inherit long-context failure modes.
This new research introduces Parallel-Distill-Refine (PDR), a framework that treats LLMs as improvement operators rather than single-pass reasoners.
Instead of one long reasoning chain, PDR operates in phases:
- Generate diverse drafts in parallel.
- Distill them into a bounded textual workspace.
- Refine conditioned on this workspace.
- Repeat.
Context length becomes controllable via degree of parallelism, no longer conflated with total tokens generated. The model accumulates wisdom across rounds through compact summaries rather than replaying full histories.
On AIME 2024, PDR achieves 93.3% accuracy compared to 79.4% for standard long chain-of-thought at matched latency budgets.
For o3-mini at 49k effective tokens, accuracy improves from 76.9% (Long CoT) to 86.7% (PDR), a 9.8 percentage point gain.
PDR also achieves the same accuracy as sequential refinement with 2.57x smaller sequential budget by converting parallel compute into accuracy without lengthening per-call context.
The researchers also trained an 8B model with operator-consistent RL to make training match the PDR inference interface. Mixing standard and operator RL yields an additional 5% improvement on both AIME benchmarks.
Bounded memory iteration can substitute for long reasoning traces while holding latency fixed. Strategic parallelism and distillation is shown to beat brute-force sequence extension.

I exactly know how to make Arena allocator work exciting for people to read
2014: This was my first project that I colead with Chris Fallin with many support from Sanjay and Jeff (while never meeting in person) as well as Greg Pike. This project caused raining of spot bonuses at google at me, and ability to move to any team which i spent on moving to research and working on optimization (not code! But neural network training)
There were a tonne of clever optimizations at Google scale. A trip down memory lane, and all of this is OSS - I can proly look up and document it.
I was increasingly just spending my time optimizing google servers (largely from boredom given I wanted to work on ML and didnt have the cred to do ML yet). google wide profiling shows anybody at the company where the cpu time is spent and code is all open for anyone to read. This lead to finding that most of Google servers (sometimes upto 50%) spent time on allocated, deallocate, serialize and deserialize. Tcmalloc did a good job, but protobuf design with its many level trees meant death by a hundred thousand cuts.
Arena allocator sounded like a good idea, so I picked up some prototype that was not working yet from Liu Jisi and optimized it. First on the menu was speeding up thre destructor chain with destructor skippable trait/ SIFNAE - this showed signs of life and we sent the benchmarks to the protobuf mailing list which got everyone interested.
In a short 4 month sprint during the summer of 2024, all I did was write code to get Arena work for Google with Chris. Good times!
It has stayed the test of time at Google. Every single rpc goes through it, probably saved google O(10b) dollars on machine costs.
Here is the very fast arena allocator
Code still looks nice! Few clever things
- PerThread Arena for avoiding contention
- AlignedAlloc Fast Path!
- Skipping chain destructors for large depth
- custom string instead of std::string which we got a lot of flak for, but was needed for performance
We did several clever things to integrate it to existing protobuf and make sure no servers fail over
* low level optimization of generated code to balance binary size and run time. This is where Geoff Pike showed his brilliance!
* Sanjay’s continued bithacking brilliance with unknownfieldset packing of arena ptr to save 4 bytes per protobuf which was a blocker in integration
Martin who was initially using it for Play Servers fixed one of the perf problems inside arena but I don’t remember it yet.

title: Anirudh Goyal (@anirudhg9119) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] Why do complex skills “emerge” in bigger LLMs?
LLM “emergence” isn’t magic. Our work shows it’s a mathematical consequence of (1) scaling laws + (2) how real text mixes skills.
We call it slingshot generalisation.
Work with @prfsanjeevarora
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G-qTY9FbQAcg6Nt.png
Quoting @_sholtodouglas
One day we’ll be able to decompose the loss curve of a neural net into all of the quanta it learns along the way - this is one of my fav streams of fundamental research. Really promising line of work
────────
[2/10] (2/N) The mystery: as models scale, they suddenly do new tasks (reasoning, compositional stuff, etc.).
Mechanistic explanations via SGD dynamics are hard. So: we try a macro theory instead.
────────
[3/10] (3/N) Key intuition: model language as a skill graph.
Bipartite graph:
• left = latent “skills”
• right = “text-pieces”
Edge = this text-piece requires that skill.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G-qToEoaoAAIWXx.jpg
────────
[4/10] (5/N) Now connect this to what we actually optimize: cross-entropy loss. Scaling laws tell us how loss drops as we scale parameters + data.
If normal text already blends multiple skills, then “getting low loss” forces you to learn lots of underlying skills — not just memorize.
────────
[5/10] (4/N) How do we test “understanding” of a text-piece?
Insert simple cloze multiple-choice questions at test time.
Competence = success rate on those cloze questions.
5
(@ilyasut also talks about it).
────────
[6/10] (8/N) If you scale a model so its loss drops by about 1/k′, then its predicted performance curve on k′-tuples matches the earlier curve for single skills.
────────
[7/10] (7/N) Slingshot generalization claim:
Competence on skill combinations (k-tuples) improves almost as fast as competence on individual skills.
Compositionality comes “for free” once loss is low enough.
────────
[8/10] (6/N) So why does emergence look “sudden”?
Because a small drop in loss can move you from “often wrong on a rare slice of text” → “rarely wrong everywhere,” which flips many skills from failing to passing.
────────
[9/10] (10/N) Why this matters:
It reframes “emergence” as a predictable outcome of (a) loss reduction + (b) combinatorial mixing in the data.
────────
[10/10] (9/N) Assume “Chinchilla-like” scaling where ~10× scaling ≈ ~2× reduction in excess loss → then you’d expect similar competence on pairs, then 4-tuples, etc., with successive scaling steps.

title: Anirudh Goyal (@anirudhg9119)
summary:
"Durable engine - one that compounds learning over time and consistently turns long-horizon exploration into real, measurable advances, while ensuring those advances become valuable"
Valid for research labs, as well as for agents.
"Scaling by Compounding Experience"
Quoting @markchen90
How does OpenAI balance long-term research bets with product-forward research fundamentals?
I’ve been getting this question a lot lately, usually framed as a suggestion that Jakub (@merettm) and I are pushing an increasingly product-focused agenda.
That characterization is simply wrong. Foundational research has been core to OpenAI from the start, and today we run a research program with hundreds of exploratory projects - much like the ones that led to our reasoning-model breakthrough. The majority of our compute is allocated to foundational research and exploration - and not product milestones.
Anyone who has spent time with me or Jakub knows we are the last people in the world who would push for the advancement of products over the advancement of research. We’re in the business of creating an automated scientist, and capabilities that were considered grand challenges just a few years ago (like IMO-level mathematical reasoning) now emerge as normal parts of the research process. We’re also seeing our models accelerate researchers worldwide, helping advance work across biology, mathematics, physics, and even our own research.
Jakub and I put a lot of effort into ensuring that research stays focused on uncovering algorithms that will scale to the compute we’ll have a year from now. We protect mindshare and amplify discourse on exploratory work. We do this while recognizing that we’re also a deployment company - and that deployment gives us access to even larger-scale compute, richer feedback, and more room for exploration. Our researchers are passionate about having their work out in the world, and a special slice of our org is dedicated to making sure our deployments are delightful for end users.
Our goal isn’t to turn research into a quarterly race. It’s to build a durable research engine - one that compounds learning over time and consistently turns long-horizon exploration into real, measurable advances, while ensuring those advances become valuable in the real world. That’s the roadmap we’re executing on. And while there have been ups and downs over the last decade (as you expect with any research program), I think most of our researchers would share my strong optimism today.

summary:
[1/3] New work: Escaping the Cognitive Well — how to solve IMO-style proof problems efficiently with off-the-shelf LLMs.
Key failure we target: iterative solver↔grader loops can converge to a plausible but wrong proof that the grader starts “believing” (the cognitive well).
Quoting @prfsanjeevarora
From @PrincetonPLI New, low-cost, and fully open "deep thinking" for LLMs to solve competition math questions. State-of-the-art 64.8% at IMO-Bench (Advanced) for $31/question, and 52% for $3/question. By contrast, DeepSeek’s published recipe allowed up to $3K/question for 61.7%! Key idea: how to nudge an LLM to escape its “Cognitive Well”
@xingyudang, Rohit Agarwal, @liam_fowl, Rodrigo Porto, @anirudhg9119
────────
[2/3] When progress stalls, don’t refine in the same context. Extract conjectures/lemmas that the current proof depends on, then do contextual detachment: verify each lemma (and its negation) in fresh context. If ¬lemma is provable, we’ve diagnosed the whole direction as doomed.
────────
[3/3] Result: on IMO-ProofBench Advanced (PB-Adv) we report 67.1% with Gemini 3.0 Pro at about $31/problem—positioning it as a strong accuracy-per-$ point vs heavier pipelines.
Takeaway: add an explicit “decontaminate verification” operator to escape local minima in agent loops.

title: Anirudh Goyal (@anirudhg9119) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] (Current) LLM-based ideation is biased toward what the field already finds easy to think.
Here, we formalize that bias as cognitive availability, and use it to search for coherent but under-reachable research directions. 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDaHtPyXMAA8rfx.jpg
────────
[2/5] That suggests a different target for AI-assisted discovery.
Not just “generate novel ideas.”
Instead: search for directions that are simultaneously
high in coherence
low in cognitive availability
This is the region of idea space we call alien.
────────
[3/5] The key distinction is between two quantities:
- coherence: does a combination of concepts form a viable research direction?
- cognitive availability: how likely is that direction to be naturally proposed by a typical researcher, given what they have worked on?
────────
[4/5] On top of that representation, we "train" two separate models:
a coherence model, which scores whether a set of atoms forms a plausible direction
an availability model, which scores how likely that direction is to be generated by researchers drawn from the community
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDaIafkWwAACwFu.jpg
────────
[5/5] What I find most interesting is:
A lot of current “AI for research” work focuses on accelerating search within regions humans already traverse well.
This frames a different problem: Can AI help us explore coherent regions that are systematically hard for the field to reach?

summary:
[1/8] (1/N) How should we evaluate AI agents that conduct ML research?
Final performance tells us whether an agent succeeded, but not how it searched.
In this work, we analyze AI research agents through the lens of search dynamics.
. .
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJRvDj2aUAAQoQ1.jpg
────────
[2/8] (2/N) Current AI research agents bundle many things together: search strategy, code editor, experiment runner, memory system, validation loop.
So when one agent wins, we often don’t know what actually caused the win.
Was it better research strategy or better infrastructure?
────────
[3/8] (4/N) We analyze:
18 ML research tasks,
10 domains,
real public research codebases,
held-out test evaluation,
and 12 process-level metrics.
So we can study not only how much an agent improves performance, but how it moves through the research landscape.
────────
[4/8] (3/N) In this work, we isolate the thing we care about:
agent strategy.
We keep the execution infrastructure shared, while letting agents differ in how they generate ideas, choose experiments, remember results, and decide what to try next.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJRvv3waQAA_PzS.jpg
────────
[5/8] (5/N) The first interesting behaviour:
A simple greedy hill-climber nearly matches the best tree-search agent.
This is interesting, as more complicated scaffolding does not automatically produce better research behavior.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJRwHEabgAEnecm.jpg
────────
[6/8] (7/N) This suggests a simple principle:
AI research agents should not use a fixed search strategy. They should adapt online.
Exploit when progress is easy.
Explore when progress stalls.
Our AdaptiveSearch agent implements this idea and outperforms the fixed strategies.
────────
[7/8] (9/N) To me, the main message is:
The next generation of AI research agents will be systems that understand the dynamics of research search: when to exploit, when to explore, when to switch, and when to stop.
────────
[8/8] (10/N) This work is a step toward making AI research agents scientifically measurable i.e. controlled evaluation of the mechanisms that make agents better researchers.

summary:
[1/5] AI research agents have a new bottleneck: they can invent experiments much faster than they can afford to run them.
Our new work asks: can an agent decide which ideas are worth the GPU time before executing them?
Introducing AI Research Preference Models (RPMs) 🧵
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2094780103058149376/img/mJsBfxWXBAfDmdWc.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2094780103058149376/vid/avc1/480x270/cQhf27XXg9cCzxny.mp4?tag=14
────────
[2/5] The problem is simple:
Generating a new ML idea/code change can take minutes.
Testing it may require hours or days of GPU compute.
So if an agent proposes 15 ideas but can run only 1, research progress depends heavily on choosing the right 1.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HRIoWIfWEAAO2mb.jpg
────────
[3/5] Instead of predicting the exact score an experiment will achieve (a hard forecasting problem), we turn this into a preference problem:
Given several candidate solutions + the research history so far, rank which candidate is most worth executing next.
────────
[4/5] The broader lesson:
For AI research agents, test-time compute shouldn’t only generate more ideas. It can also decide which ideas deserve real experiments.
In expensive-search domains, intelligence is partly knowing what not to run.
Paper:
────────
[5/5] A few scaling results stood out:
• More history → better selection
• More reasoning → better selection
• Larger candidate pools → more upside
• Pilot experiments help, with diminishing returns
In other words: selection quality itself scales with compute.

title: Anirudh Goyal (@anirudhg9119) — thread (11 tweets)
summary:
[1/11] What if an agent could decide how to structure its own computation?
Agentic Meta-Reasoning: Let the model decide what to explore, what to build on, what to verify, and where to spend its next unit of compute: effectively constructing its own computational graph as it reasons. 🧵
Paras Dahal, @anton_bakhtin , @TacoCohen , Zhengxing Chen, Carole-Jean Wu, Rob Fergus, Scott Yih, @syhw , @rsalakhu , @prfsanjeevarora , @jaseweston
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTfBnkTbQAAtBPp.jpg
────────
[2/11] 2/
As agents take on longer and harder problems, execution itself becomes a reasoning problem.
At every step, the agent must decide how to allocate compute:
Breadth: explore a new direction?
Depth: invest further in a promising one?
Verification: check or revise existing work?
Stopping: is further computation worth it?
The longer the run, the more consequential these choices become.
────────
[3/11] 4/
Instead of executing a fixed reasoning loop, the agent can dynamically construct its own computational graph.
It decides when to branch, when to deepen a path, when to revisit earlier work, and which artifacts should become context for what comes next.
The structure of inference becomes something the model reasons about.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTfDZbzaYAAEjHJ.jpg
────────
[4/11] 3/
This suggests separating two kinds of reasoning:
Object-level reasoning: solve the task.
Meta-reasoning: decide how the computation used to solve the task should unfold.
One produces the work. The other shapes the search over work.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTfDcxsbAAAJyZA.jpg
────────
[5/11] 6/
Does explicit control over computation matter?
Across different models and task domains, structuring inference through meta-reasoning leads to stronger final outcomes.
The broader claim is simple: Inference performance depends not only on how much compute you have, but on how that compute is organized.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTfCHPLakAEDdb4.jpg
────────
[6/11] 5/
This also changes how context is managed.
Past work is stored as persistent artifacts rather than repeatedly replayed as one growing transcript.
The controller carries a compact view of the run and retrieves the pieces that matter for the next decision.
So long-horizon reasoning becomes stateful without requiring the full history in context.
────────
[7/11] 7/
This becomes especially important as the inference budget grows.
Extra compute creates more possible actions: more branches to explore, more paths to deepen, more results to verify.
Without good control, a larger budget can simply create more opportunities to spend compute poorly.
Meta-reasoning turns compute scaling into an allocation problem. What is the most useful thing I can do with the compute I have left?
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTfCO6haoAA4lbN.png
────────
[8/11] 9/
There is another control problem hiding inside long reasoning runs:
Finding useful work is not the same as recognizing useful work.
A worker may produce a strong intermediate result without knowing how much to trust it.
A separate controller can assess that work and decide whether to build on it, verify it, or move elsewhere.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTfCgNib0AAIDUG.jpg
────────
[9/11] 8/
And you can see that allocation in the computation itself. The agent doesn’t just generate a longer trajectory.
It creates a structured graph where later work can branch from, verify, repair, or synthesize earlier work.
More inference can produce more structure: not just more tokens or "more attempts".
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTfCUSTacAAR1J5.png
────────
[10/11] 11/
That’s the idea behind:
Thinking Before Thinking: Scaling Agentic Inference Through Meta-Reasoning
Make the execution strategy itself part of the reasoning process.
arXiv artifact:
────────
[11/11] 10/
This suggests a different way to think about inference-time scaling.
Not just: How much computation should we run?
But: What computation should we run, how should it depend on what came before, and when should we stop?
Scaling reasoning may increasingly mean scaling the ability to structure computation itself.
